analysis.investment_thesis: Campus is India's largest domestic sports footwear brand with genuine ROCE of 31.8% and improving FCF, but operating margins have structurally compressed from 20.3% (FY22) to 11.5% (FY25), and the market is asking you to pay 55x earnings for that deteriorating profitability — a classic case of a decent business at a decidedly indecent price.
key_strengths: ROCE of 31.8% demonstrates real capital efficiency in a competitive footwear market
FCF/Net Income of 145% (₹176 Cr / ₹121 Cr in FY25) confirms high-quality earnings with no accounting games
Debt/EBITDA of only 0.9x (₹232 Cr debt vs ₹259 Cr EBITDA) — balance sheet risk is contained
key_risks: Severe margin compression: operating margin fell from 20.3% in FY22 → 11.5% in FY25, suggesting pricing power erosion under competitive pressure from Nike, Adidas, and domestic discounters
Revenue stagnation in the mass-market segment — FY24 revenue actually declined (₹1,448 Cr vs ₹1,484 Cr in FY23), with FY25 recovery only modest
55x P/E is pricing in perfection; any further margin slip or growth disappointment will destroy significant market cap
red_flags: Secular operating margin decline over 3 consecutive years (FY22–FY25) — classic sign of weak pricing power
Net profit of ₹121 Cr in FY25 still barely exceeds FY23's ₹117 Cr — two years of zero earnings growth at 55x P/E is indefensible
Value-segment footwear has no durable moat — easily disrupted by better-funded global brands or private-label e-commerce
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Campus occupies an interesting niche — India's largest domestic sports footwear brand by volume, serving the mass-to-mid market. ROCE of 31.8% and clean FCF generation (₹176 Cr FCF vs ₹121 Cr net profit in FY25) are genuinely commendable. Promoter holding of 72% suggests alignment. However, applying Munger's inversion: what could permanently impair this business? The answer is obvious — margin erosion from competition, which is already happening. Operating margins have collapsed from 20.3% in FY22 to 11.5% in FY25. That is not a cyclical blip; it is a structural squeeze as global brands deepen Indian distribution and e-commerce commoditizes footwear pricing.

The valuation commits the most grievous investment sin: paying 55x P/E for a business whose earnings have essentially flatlined for two years (₹117 Cr FY23 → ₹89 Cr FY24 → ₹121 Cr FY25). At EV/EBITDA of 33x, the market is extrapolating a compounding machine that the fundamentals do not yet support. A business in a commoditizing segment, with declining margins and no defensible moat beyond brand familiarity, deserves a 20–25x multiple at best. At ₹248, I would need to see sustained margin recovery above 16%+ and consistent double-digit revenue growth before reconsidering. The current price offers no margin of safety whatsoever — and margin of safety is the cornerstone of sensible investing.
